t: Add Minimum Number of Rungs: Greedy Gap Filling with Arithmetic
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Starting on the floor at height 0, you climb a strictly increasing ladder of rung heights, and each move may rise at most dist; you may insert rungs at any unused positive integer height and must finish on the last rung. Because the rungs only go up, the climb is forced left to right: for every consecutive pair of positions you simply need enough intermediate steps so no single jump exceeds dist. In Example 1 ([1,3,5,10], dist = 2) the final jump 5 -> 10 forces inserted rungs at 7 and 8. In Example 2 all gaps are at most 3, so nothing is added. In Example 3 the very first leap 0 -> 3 already exceeds dist = 2, forcing a rung at height 1 — the floor counts as a position. Heights reach 10^9, so inserting one rung per iteration can take billions of loop turns; closing each gap with one arithmetic expression is essential.
k: Gaps are independent: crossing a gap of size g needs ceil(g/dist) - 1 inserted rungs, after which you stand exactly on the far rung.
In integer arithmetic ceil(g/dist) - 1 equals (g - 1) / dist (floor division), avoiding floating point entirely.
Placing each inserted rung as high as legally possible (every dist units from your current height) is optimal — a higher standing point never hurts the remaining gaps.

a.i: Model climbing literally: keep your current height cur and, whenever the next rung is out of reach, insert one rung exactly dist above cur and step onto it. Repeat until the next real rung is reachable. This is the most direct translation of the rules and obviously minimal per move, but its running time is proportional to the number of added rungs, which can be enormous when heights are large and dist is small.
s: For each rung h in increasing order:
While h - cur > dist, add a rung at cur + dist, step there (cur += dist), increment added.
a.t: O(n + A) where A is the number of added rungs — correct but A reaches ~10^9 when dist = 1 and heights are large, causing timeouts.

a.i: Replace the inner while loop by counting: a gap g between consecutive standing points requires exactly ceil(g/dist) - 1 new rungs, since you advance dist per inserted rung before landing on the far side. Sum this over all gaps, treating the floor (height 0) as the starting point. Each gap costs O(1), so total work is linear regardless of magnitudes.
s: For each rung height h compute gap = h - prev.
If gap > dist, add (gap - 1) / dist (integer division) to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — one constant-time computation per gap.

w: Present Approach 2 directly; use Approach 1 only to demonstrate understanding or when constraints are tiny. Pitfalls: forgetting that you start on the floor (Example 3's gap 0 -> 3 must be counted), using floating-point ceiling functions that lose precision near 10^9, and 32-bit overflow when multiplying or subtracting large heights in C++/Java — widen to 64-bit. Note dist itself is reachable (at most dist is allowed). Follow-ups: minimum insertions if you may also remove rungs, maximizing reachable height with a budget of k insertions, or handling non-integer allowed heights.
